problem.title: On-device visual inspection
problem.context: A manufacturer inspects parts for defects with cameras along its production lines. There are 40 lines in three plants, each with two to four cameras attached to a small edge computer next to the line. The plants' network is unreliable: some lines are cut off for days at a time. Quality inspectors label images of defects, about 5,000 new labels a week, and the model is retrained every week from them and pushed to the devices. The team is two ML engineers and one person who spends half their time on operations. The infrastructure budget is tight.

requirements.text: Check every part as it passes the camera and signal a defective part to the line operator.
Retrain the model every week from the newly labelled images and roll the new model out to every line.
Collect the images the model was unsure about, or got wrong, so that inspectors can label them.
Each image is classified on the line within 200 ms, so the line never slows down.
When a plant's network is down for up to seven days, its lines keep inspecting with the model they have; the images collected in the meantime are uploaded when the network returns.
A new model reaches every connected line within 24 hours of approval. When a new model misbehaves on a line, the line operator can go back to the previous one within 15 minutes, without the ML team.
Cloud and infrastructure spending stays under 2,000 euros a month.
Three people build and run the system, with no support outside working hours.
The edge computers (an ARM processor with a small neural accelerator) cannot be replaced this year.

Training: Managed weekly cloud retraining

Fleet control: Managed cloud device fleet
Model rollout: Signed staged rollout with local rollback
points.description: Devices perform inference locally, while inspection data is held in a durable queue and uploaded resumably when connectivity permits. A managed cloud fleet coordinates weekly retraining and distributes signed models through staged rollouts, with devices able to roll back locally. Trade-off: This provides offline-capable, low-latency inference and controlled model deployment. It gives up immediate access to newly collected data for training and requires local storage and operational handling of queued data; fleet management and retraining also depend on eventual connectivity.

points.description: Inspection devices perform inference locally, while a plant gateway persistently spools offline data for later upload to the managed cloud retraining process. The gateway coordinates devices and caches staged model rollouts, allowing local rollback while distributing updated models without sending inference to the cloud. Trade-off: This preserves operation during connectivity loss and enables controlled plant-level deployment, but models may remain stale between weekly retraining or delayed uploads, while gateway coordination and spool storage add operational overhead. It gives up centralized, real-time fleet control in favor of plant-local autonomy.

Trade-off: This favors low-latency, offline-capable inspection and controlled, reversible deployment, but gives up immediate model updates and centralized push control; polling and weekly retraining introduce delay. It also requires local storage and coordination for queues and model slots.

points.description: **Solution:** Devices run inference locally and capture images when uncertainty or errors occur, buffering them in a durable queue for resumable upload while remaining under managed cloud fleet control. The cloud retrains models weekly, then uses automated, health-gated canary rollout, with each device able to roll back locally. **Trade-off:** This gains responsive, resilient inspection and controlled fleet updates, but requires local queueing, monitoring, and rollback machinery; triggered image uploads also consume storage and bandwidth, while weekly retraining may lag changing conditions.

approaches.idea: What if managed cloud fleet services automate staging, health checks, and rollback while edge devices hold the line offline?
What if each plant gateway provides local coordination, caching, and store-and-forward autonomy?
What if devices pull low-cost object-storage artifacts directly and operators advance tested rollout waves?
What if gateways only buffer selected images while cloud-managed devices fetch models directly?

adrs.title: Where should inspection inference run?
adrs.context: Every part must be inspected within 200 ms while production continues through week-long plant network outages. The ARM edge computers cannot be replaced this year, so inference must use the installed devices and be validated against their accelerator and model capacity.

options.name: Edge-only inference
values: Inference: Edge-only on-device inference
pros: Inspection remains available without cloud connectivity.
The network is not on the per-image classification path.
cons: The model must fit and meet the latency target on the existing ARM accelerator.
options.reason: All four alternatives preserve line operation during outages and avoid replacing the constrained edge computers.

adrs.title: How should selected images feed weekly retraining?
adrs.context: Inspectors label about 5,000 new defect images weekly, and retraining must use new labels. Images need to survive network outages, while storing and uploading all camera traffic would increase bandwidth and storage needs. Capture should focus on uncertain or incorrect predictions.

options.name: Managed weekly training with selective capture
values: Training: Managed weekly cloud retraining
Capture policy: Uncertainty and error-triggered image capture
pros: Targets inspector effort and image transfer at informative or incorrect cases.
cons: Training reflects uploaded samples and may lag live production changes.
options.reason: This covers weekly model updates and the requested feedback loop while limiting unnecessary image collection.

options.name: Device queues with resumable upload
values: Offline data: Durable local queue with resumable upload
pros: Each device can retain samples independently through outages.
cons: Queue capacity and fleet-wide upload behavior need sizing.
options.reason: This keeps buffering close to the cameras without introducing plant gateway storage operations.

options.name: Per-camera queues relayed through plant gateway
values: Offline data: Per-camera durable queues relayed through gateway
pros: Camera queues reduce dependence on one plant spool.
The gateway can consolidate deferred uploads.
cons: Many local queues and gateway relay add operations.
options.reason: This preserves data during connectivity loss while reducing a gateway spool as a single storage dependency.

options.name: Persistent gateway spool
values: Offline data: Plant gateway persistent spool with deferred upload
pros: A single plant buffer can store selected images and upload later.
Keeps bulk data transfer separate from inference.
cons: Gateway storage and capacity become important dependencies.
options.reason: This centralizes data relay without making the gateway responsible for model rollout.

adrs.title: How should models reach lines and recover from bad releases?
adrs.context: Approved models must reach every connected line within 24 hours, and operators must be able to restore a previous model within 15 minutes without the ML team. Rollouts must fit a small operations allocation and a tight infrastructure budget.
